records.question: Under the enacted provisions of Section 4(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027 under G.S.R. 843(E)), under what grounds may personal data be processed?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 4(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (enacted and scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027 under Notification G.S.R. 843(E), and not yet in force as of 16 October 2026), a person may process the personal data of a Data Principal only in accordance with the provisions of this Act and for a lawful purpose: (a) for which the Data Principal has given her consent; or (b) for certain legitimate uses.
statutory_citations: Section 4(1), Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

evidence_passages.verbatim_text:
4. Grounds for processing personal data.-(1) A person may process the personal data of a Data Principal only in accordance with the provisions of this Act and for a lawful purpose,-

(a) for which the Data Principal has given her consent; or

- (b) for certain legitimate uses.

supporting_sources.title: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act No. 22 of 2023)

records.question: What statutory notice requirements are mandated under the enacted text of Section 5(1) of the DPDP Act, 2023 when requesting consent from a Data Principal once commenced?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 5(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (enacted and appointed to commence on 13 May 2027 under G.S.R. 843(E), hence uncommenced as of 16 October 2026), every request made to a Data Principal under Section 6 for consent shall be accompanied or preceded by a notice informing her: (i) the personal data and the purpose for which the same is proposed to be processed; (ii) the manner in which she may exercise her rights under Section 6(4) and Section 13; and (iii) the manner in which she may make a complaint to the Board.
statutory_citations: Section 5(1), Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

supporting_sources.title: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act No. 22 of 2023)

records.question: When may personal data be processed for legitimate uses under the enacted scheme of Section 7(a) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 upon its scheduled commencement?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 7(a) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (enacted and scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027 under G.S.R. 843(E) and not yet in force as of 16 October 2026), a Data Fiduciary may process personal data of a Data Principal for the specified purpose for which the Data Principal has voluntarily provided her personal data to the Data Fiduciary, and in respect of which she has not indicated to the Data Fiduciary that she does not consent to the use of her personal data.
statutory_citations: Section 7(a), Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

evidence_passages.verbatim_text:
7. Certain legitimate uses.-A Data Fiduciary may process personal data of a Data Principal for any of following uses, namely:-

(a) for the specified purpose for which the Data Principal has voluntarily provided her personal data to the Data Fiduciary, and in respect of which she has not indicated to the Data Fiduciary that she does not consent to the use of her personal data.

supporting_sources.title: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act No. 22 of 2023)

records.question: What statutory consent requirement applies to processing personal data of children under the enacted Section 9(1) of the DPDP Act, 2023 when it takes effect?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 9(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027 under Notification G.S.R. 843(E) and uncommenced as of 16 October 2026), the Data Fiduciary shall, before processing any personal data of a child or a person with disability who has a lawful guardian, obtain verifiable consent of the parent of such child or the lawful guardian, as the case may be, in such manner as may be prescribed.
statutory_citations: Section 9(1), Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

evidence_passages.verbatim_text: 9. Processing of personal data of children.-(1) The Data Fiduciary shall, before processing any personal data of a child or a person with disability who has a lawful guardian obtain verifiable consent of the parent of such child or the lawful guardian, as the case may be, in such manner as may be prescribed.

records.question: What assessment factors guide the Central Government in notifying a Significant Data Fiduciary under the enacted Section 10(1) of the DPDP Act, 2023?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 10(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (enacted and scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027 under G.S.R. 843(E), not yet in force as of 16 October 2026), the Central Government may notify any Data Fiduciary or class of Data Fiduciaries as Significant Data Fiduciary based on assessment of factors including: (a) the volume and sensitivity of personal data processed; (b) risk to the rights of Data Principal; and (c) potential impact on the sovereignty and integrity of India.
statutory_citations: Section 10(1), Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

supporting_sources.title: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act No. 22 of 2023)

records.question: Under what circumstances may a police officer arrest a person without a warrant under Section 35(1)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023?

records.question: How may information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence be given to a police station under Section 173(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 173(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under Notification S.O. 848(E)), every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, irrespective of the area where the offence is committed, may be given orally or by electronic communication to an officer in charge of a police station.

records.question: What statutory right to bail is provided to an under-trial prisoner who has undergone detention extending up to one-half of the maximum sentence under Section 479(1) of the BNSS 2023?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 479(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under Notification S.O. 848(E)), where a person has, during the period of investigation, inquiry, or trial of an offence (not being an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment) undergone detention extending up to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence, he shall be released by the Court on bail.

records.question: What is the scope of inherent powers preserved for the High Court under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under S.O. 848(E)), nothing in the Sanhita shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Sanhita, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

records.question: What repeal and savings effect does Section 531(1) and 531(2)(a) of the BNSS 2023 have on proceedings instituted under the CrPC 1973 prior to 1 July 2024?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 531(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under S.O. 848(E)), the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is repealed. However, by virtue of Section 531(2)(a), any appeal, application, trial, inquiry, or investigation pending immediately before 1 July 2024 shall be disposed of, continued, held, or made in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 as if the BNSS had not come into force.

records.question: What statutory rule of admissibility is established for electronic or digital records under Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under Notification S.O. 849(E)), nothing in this Adhiniyam shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic or digital record in the evidence on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record, and such record shall have the same legal effect, validity and enforceability as other document, subject to the provisions of Section 63.

evidence_passages.verbatim_text: Nothing in this Adhiniyam shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic or digital record in the evidence on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record, and such record shall have the same legal effect, validity and enforceability as other document, subject to the provisions of section 63.

records.question: When is electronic information stored in magnetic media deemed to be a document under Section 63(1) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023?

records.question: What minimum and maximum punishment is prescribed for penetrative sexual assault under Section 4(1) of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 4(1) of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (in force since 14 November 2012 pursuant to S.O. 2642(E)), whoever commits penetrative sexual assault shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

records.question: What enhanced punishment applies under the first proviso to Section 4 of the POCSO Act, 2012 where the child is below sixteen years of age?
records.proposed_answer: Under the first proviso to Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (in force since 14 November 2012), whoever commits penetrative sexual assault on a child below sixteen years of age shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than twenty years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of natural life of that person, and shall also be liable to fine.

records.question: What punishment is prescribed for intentionally capturing or publishing images of a private area under Section 66E of the Information Technology Act, 2000?

records.question: What is the constitutional ratio decidendi regarding the right to privacy established in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1?
records.proposed_answer: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1, the nine-judge Constitution Bench held that the right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
case_citations: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1

evidence_passages.verbatim_text: RATIO DECIDENDI: The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.

supporting_sources.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1

records.question: Which earlier Supreme Court decisions holding that privacy is not a fundamental right were overruled by the 9-Judge Bench in Puttaswamy (2017) 10 SCC 1?
records.proposed_answer: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1, the nine-judge Constitution Bench expressly overruled the earlier decisions in M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954) SCR 1077 and Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1964) 1 SCR 332 to the extent that they had held privacy is not a fundamental right under the Constitution.
